screening_decisions.reason: Randomised controlled trial in women with stress urinary incontinence. One arm received pelvic floor muscle exercises, another arm received no exercises. Meets all selection criteria.

Randomised controlled trial in women with SUI. The intervention arm used a mobile app that delivered PFMT (98.4% of intervention participants performed PFMT at follow-up). The control arm was postponed treatment, an inactive control. Meets selection criteria.
Randomised controlled trial in postmenopausal women with SUI. Included PFME alone and PFME + biofeedback arms, plus a control group assessed without active treatment. Meets selection criteria.

The intervention arm is biofeedback-assisted behavioral treatment, not explicitly pelvic floor muscle training. The review specifically requires an arm that included PFMT; this study compares behavioral therapy versus drug versus placebo for urge/mixed UI without clearly specifying a PFMT arm.
Randomised controlled trial in older women with stress incontinence. Arms included biofeedback, pelvic muscle exercise (PFMT), and a control group. Meets selection criteria.
Randomised controlled trial in women with urodynamically proven genuine stress incontinence. Included a pelvic floor exercise arm and an untreated control group. Meets selection criteria.

Experimental study with 50 women with SUI randomly distributed into an exercise group (pelvic floor exercises) and a control group. Although the abstract calls it an experimental study, participants were randomly allocated and a control group was included. Conservative inclusion applied.
Randomised controlled trial in women with urodynamic stress urinary incontinence. Included a pelvic floor exercises arm and a no treatment (untreated control) arm. Meets selection criteria.

Prospective randomised controlled trial in women with stress and mixed urinary incontinence. Compared a pelvic floor muscle training group with a control group performing no treatment. Meets selection criteria.

Randomised controlled trial in women with UI. The treatment group received a behavioral modification program that included pelvic floor muscle training (evidenced by significant improvements in pelvic muscle strength). The control group received no treatment. Conservative inclusion applied because PFMT is a component of the intervention arm.

The abstract describes a prospective randomised study of physical therapy but does not mention a no-treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control arm. Without evidence of an inactive comparator, this study does not meet the selection criteria.

Randomised controlled crossover trial in elderly women with SUI. The intervention group performed pelvic floor muscle and fitness exercises, while the control group showed no significant changes, indicating an inactive control. Meets selection criteria.

Randomised trial in elderly women with stress, urge, and mixed UI. Included an exercise-only arm (PFMT) and an education-only control group, which qualifies as an inactive control. Meets selection criteria.

Randomised controlled trial in elderly women with stress, urge, and mixed UI. The intervention group received multidimensional exercise treatment including pelvic floor exercise; the control group showed no significant improvement, indicating an inactive control. Meets selection criteria.

Controlled trial in older women with stress, urge, or mixed UI. The intervention included pelvic floor muscle training with manual palpation and verbal feedback. The control group received advice and an educational pamphlet, an inactive control. Meets selection criteria.

Randomised trial in women with SUI. The treatment group received physiotherapist-supervised pelvic floor muscle training and a home exercise program; the control group received no treatment. Meets selection criteria.

Prospective randomised interventional study in women with SUI. The intervention group was taught a pelvic floor muscle contraction skill ('The Knack'); the control group was wait-listed. Wait-list controls qualify as inactive controls. Conservative inclusion applied.
Randomised controlled pilot study in women with SUI. Included group PFMT, individual PFMT, and a control group receiving no treatment. Meets selection criteria.
Randomised trial in women with mixed UI. Included a PFMT arm and a waiting list control group. Waiting list is an inactive control. Meets selection criteria.

Randomised controlled trial in postmenopausal women with UI. The intervention was physical therapy for UI, which in standard practice for this population includes PFMT as the primary component. The control was osteoporosis education, an inactive control for UI. Conservative inclusion applied given the typical composition of PT for UI.

The study compared bladder training and pelvic muscle exercise against a control group in women with urinary incontinence. The pelvic muscle exercise arm qualifies as PFMT, and the abstract mentions a control group. Conservative inclusion applied due to limited abstract detail.

Experimental study in women with SUI randomly divided into groups. Included a kinesitherapy group (pelvic floor muscle exercise) and a control group. Kinesitherapy represents PFMT. Conservative inclusion applied.

Experimental study with female athletes randomly allocated to groups. The experimental group underwent a pelvic floor muscles rehabilitation program (PFMRP), and the control group had only access to a pamphlet. The athletes had stress urinary incontinence. The pamphlet-only group is an inactive control. Meets selection criteria.

Randomised trial in women with genuine stress incontinence. Included pelvic floor exercises, interferential therapy, oestrogen, and a control group. The control group showed no significant changes, indicating an inactive control. Meets selection criteria.
Controlled trial in women with genuine stress incontinence. The treatment group received pelvic floor exercises, and the control group received no therapy. Meets selection criteria.

Parallel-group RCT in women with stress or mixed UI. One arm received PFM training (including fast/slow contractions and the knack) and the untreated control group had no contact during the 8-week intervention period. This is PFMT versus no-treatment, meeting all selection criteria.

This is a care-delivery model trial (nurse specialist involvement in primary care versus usual care by GPs), not a direct PFMT versus inactive-control trial. The intervention is organizational and both arms may include mixed treatments; the population is described as adult patients rather than specifically women with SUI/UUI/MUI.
This reports consumer-satisfaction data from the same nurse-specialist care-delivery RCT as study 27. It is not a trial of PFMT versus an inactive control.

RCT in women with urge/mixed UI comparing biofeedback-assisted behavioral training, behavioral training without biofeedback, and a self-administered behavioral treatment using a self-help booklet. All three arms are active behavioral treatments; there is no no-treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm.
This is a feasibility study, not a randomized or quasi-randomised trial. Four treatment groups at different sites plus an education-only group; no randomization is described.
RCT comparing supervised PFMT versus unsupervised PFMT in women with SUI. Both trial arms include active PFMT; there is no no-treatment, placebo, sham, or other inactive control arm.

RCT comparing stabilization exercises focusing on pelvic floor muscles versus routine physiotherapy modalities and regular exercises for low back pain. The comparator is an active physiotherapy intervention, not no treatment or an inactive control.

RCT comparing behavioral training, behavioral training plus PFES, and a self-help booklet (control). The self-help booklet constitutes an active self-administered behavioral treatment; there is no no-treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm.

RCT in elderly women with UI residing in long-term care. The training group included Kegel’s exercise (PFMT) together with Thera-band training and indoor walking; the control group received no described intervention (implicitly no additional treatment). This meets the PFMT versus no-treatment criterion, though the control arm is not explicitly detailed.

RCT of behavioral therapy versus no therapy in women with UI. The abstract does not explicitly describe pelvic floor muscle training as part of the behavioral therapy intervention. Because the review requires that one trial arm specifically includes PFMT, this study does not clearly meet the intervention criterion.

Economic evaluation alongside an RCT that randomized women to internet-based PFMT versus postal PFMT. The underlying trial has no no-treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm; the no-treatment comparison was modelled using baseline data, not an actual trial arm.
RCT comparing internet-based PFMT versus a postal PFMT programme in women with SUI. Both arms are active PFMT interventions; there is no no-treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm.
Long-term follow-up of the same RCT as study 37 (internet-based PFMT versus postal PFMT). The underlying trial lacks a no-treatment, placebo, sham, or inactive control arm.

Small RCT in women with SUI comparing TA and PFM co-contraction exercises versus a control group. The control group received no described intervention, implying no treatment. The intervention arm included PFM exercises, meeting the PFMT criterion.

Pilot RCT in frail older women with UI. The intervention combines behavioral UI treatments, walking, and strength training without explicit mention of PFMT. Additionally, the type of UI is not specified as SUI, UUI, or MUI, so the population criterion is not clearly met.

RCT in gynecologic cancer survivors with pelvic floor dysfunction. The population is not specifically women with SUI, UUI, or MUI (pelvic floor dysfunction is broader and may include prolapse, fecal incontinence, etc.). The comparator is usual health care, which is an active control, not no treatment or an inactive control.
Questionnaire development and psychometric validation study. It is not a randomized or quasi-randomised controlled trial of an intervention.
Systematic review of RCTs, not a primary randomized controlled trial.
Systematic review of RCTs, not a primary randomized controlled trial.
Methodological paper developing reporting guidelines for nonpharmacologic RCTs. It is not a primary randomized controlled trial of PFMT.
Narrative discussion/review article. Not a randomized or quasi-randomised controlled trial.
Psychometric validation study of the I-QOL instrument using data pooled from multiple studies. Not a primary randomized controlled trial.
Instrument development and reproducibility study with 14 women. No intervention was tested; it is not an RCT.
Observational imaging study measuring pelvic floor muscle function with MRI. Not a randomized or quasi-randomised controlled trial.
Narrative review discussing theoretical mechanisms of PFMT effectiveness. Not a primary randomized controlled trial.

This is a consensus-based terminology report developed by expert committees through a Delphi-like process. It is not a randomised or quasi-randomised controlled trial and does not compare PFMT against any control arm.

Secondary analysis of the EpiLUTS cross-sectional Internet survey. This is an observational epidemiological study, not an RCT. It describes prevalence and burden of UI subtypes but includes no intervention comparison.
A review chapter discussing neurotransmitters and drug targets for voiding dysfunction. It is not a clinical trial and does not evaluate PFMT versus any control in women with UI.

The abstract explicitly states the aim is 'to review the present evidence' and 'to discuss the current literature'. This is a narrative review and discussion paper, not a primary randomised controlled trial comparing PFMT to an inactive control.

Investigates functional electrical stimulation (FES) applied to the anal sphincter for hyperreflex bladder. The intervention is FES, not PFMT, and the study design is not an RCT comparing PFMT versus an inactive control in women with SUI/UUI/MUI.

Secondary analysis of pelvic muscle data in healthy women aged 35–54. The sample consists of healthy continent women, not women with diagnosed UI, and there is no RCT design comparing PFMT to an inactive control arm.
A methodology paper providing guidance on preparing Summary of Findings tables. It is not a clinical trial and does not involve any patient population or intervention comparison.
A methodology paper on presenting continuous outcomes in GRADE evidence profiles. It is not a clinical trial and contains no patient population or PFMT intervention.
A large community-based epidemiological cross-sectional survey (EPINCONT) assessing prevalence and severity of UI. It is not an RCT and does not evaluate any intervention.
A consensus-based terminology report for female pelvic floor dysfunction. It is not a clinical trial and contains no comparison of PFMT versus an inactive control.
A brief commentary or methods paper stating that quality of interventions can affect trial results. It is not a primary RCT and provides no patient data or intervention comparison.
Cross-sectional descriptive study of women attending an incontinence clinic, measuring quality of life with the SIP questionnaire. It is not an RCT and does not compare PFMT to any control.
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis (with economic modelling) of non-surgical treatments for SUI. It synthesises 88 RCTs but is not itself a primary randomised or quasi-randomised trial.
A questionnaire development and validation study assessing psychometric properties of the Bristol Female LUTS questionnaire. It is not an RCT comparing PFMT to an inactive control.

A survey measuring willingness-to-pay for symptom reduction in patients with urge or mixed incontinence. It is an observational economic study, not an RCT with a PFMT versus inactive control comparison.
Cross-sectional analysis of the National Survey of Self-Care and Aging using multivariate logistic regression. It is an observational study, not an RCT, and evaluates no intervention.
Design and validation of a condition-specific quality of life questionnaire for women with UI. It is a measurement/psychometric study, not an RCT comparing PFMT to an inactive control.

Development and validation of the YIPS psychosocial scale. Although participants were drawn from a longitudinal RCT of a behavioural/educational intervention, this paper reports only on the scale's psychometric properties, not on the RCT's comparison of PFMT versus an inactive control.

Qualitative study evaluating content validity of the King's Health Questionnaire in patients with overactive bladder. It is a questionnaire validation study, not an RCT comparing PFMT to an inactive control.
A meta-epidemiological study examining how trial quality affects effect estimates in meta-analyses. It is not a primary RCT of PFMT versus an inactive control in women with UI.
Reporting guidelines (CONSORT statement) for parallel-group RCTs. It is a methods/guidelines document, not a clinical trial evaluating PFMT.
Cross-sectional follow-up survey assessing bother and quality of life in community-dwelling women with UI. It is an observational study, not an RCT, and does not compare PFMT to any control.

Physiological study of 10 healthy nulliparous continent women assessing pelvic muscle function and bladder neck mobility. The population is healthy without UI, and there is no RCT design or comparison of PFMT to an inactive control.
Development and validation of a severity index for epidemiological surveys, compared against pad-weighing tests. It is a measurement/methods study, not an RCT comparing PFMT to an inactive control.
Cross-sectional case-control study comparing sexual function in women with UI versus continent controls using the FSFI. It is observational, not an RCT, and does not evaluate PFMT as an intervention.
Prospective cohort study evaluating the psychometric properties of the GSE-UI questionnaire; not an RCT and contains no comparison of PFMT versus an inactive control.
Instrument development paper describing short-form versions of the IIQ and UDI; not a clinical trial and lacks any PFMT or inactive control arm.
Development and validation study of the I-QOL outcome measure; not an RCT and does not compare PFMT with an inactive control.
Validation of a quality-of-life scale in psoriasis patients; unrelated to urinary incontinence intervention trials and does not involve PFMT.
Secondary analysis of data from duloxetine placebo-controlled trials assessing questionnaire validity; not a primary RCT comparing PFMT to an inactive control.
Psychometric development paper for the HADS; no relation to urinary incontinence treatment or PFMT.

RCT in women with stress urinary incontinence. One arm received structured pelvic floor muscle exercise training (PFMT) and the other a control condition. The abstract implies the control group did not receive active PFMT, consistent with an inactive/no-treatment control, though the exact control description is limited.

Randomized study in women with stress urinary incontinence including an exercises-only group (PFMT) and a control group. In this three-arm design, the control group is implied to be untreated/inactive, making the PFMT versus control comparison eligible for review.
RCT of acupressure versus sham/usual care for SUI; the active intervention is acupressure, not PFMT, and there is no PFMT arm.
RCT comparing supervised pelvic floor exercise plus home exercise versus home exercise alone; both arms involve active PFMT, with no inactive control arm described.

Double-blind RCT in women with SUI including a PFMT-only arm and a no-active-treatment arm (imitation PFMT plus placebo). This directly compares PFMT with an inactive control and meets all selection criteria.

Qualitative interview study nested within an RCT comparing two PFMT delivery modalities (Internet-based vs postal); both arms are active PFMT, and this report presents experiences rather than trial outcomes.
Follow-up analysis of predictors of long-term success after a non-face-to-face PFMT program (Internet or brochure); no inactive control group is described.
Systematic review evaluating PFMT as an adjunct to other active treatments; not a primary trial.
Narrative review and overview of exercise physiology related to PFMT; not a primary RCT.
Descriptive anatomy and urodynamics article; not an intervention trial and contains no PFMT versus control comparison.
Development and validation of the HSCL psychiatric symptom inventory; unrelated to UI or PFMT interventions.
Chapter/review discussing conservative management options for UI and prolapse; not a primary trial.
Methodological paper discussing the intention-to-treat principle and post-randomisation exclusions; not a clinical trial of PFMT.
Systematic review (Cochrane review) on PFMT versus other active treatments; not a primary trial.
Review/communication on outcome measurement domains and reliability for lower urinary tract dysfunction; not an intervention trial.
Observational MRI cohort study nested within a quasi-experimental study; not an RCT and does not compare PFMT with an inactive control.

RCT comparing conservative treatment with versus without prior urodynamic investigation; both arms receive active conservative treatment (physiotherapy and bladder retraining), so there is no PFMT-only versus inactive control comparison.
Observational pathophysiology study in institutionalized elderly men and women; not an RCT and does not evaluate PFMT versus an inactive control.
Cochrane systematic review on PFMT in antenatal and postnatal women; not a primary trial.
